Abstract
Depression detection in digital terrain analysis is crucial for surface process modelling. High-resolution satellite imagery 
has led to an increasing demand for processing ultra-large-scale digital elevation models (DEMs) with billions of grid 
cells, which has exposed the computational inefficiencies of traditional priority-flood algorithms based on priority 
queues. While existing research has primarily focused on reducing the data volume in priority-flood’s priority queues, 
few studies have focused on optimizing the sorting mechanism within these queues. In this paper, we propose a hybrid 
Hash Red Black Tree (HRBTree) data structure, integrating the efficient insertion capability of hash tables with the 
ordered key-value maintenance of the RBTree, thereby reconstructing the priority queue architecture of the priority-flood 
algorithm. Using multi-scale DEM datasets ranging from millions to 1.6 billion grid cells, we systematically evaluated 
the computational efficiency of the enhanced priority-flood algorithm across varying data scales. The experimental 
results demonstrate that the proposed HRBTree structure exhibits superior adaptability, particularly in ultra-large-scale 
datasets (> 1 billion nodes), achieving a maximum speedup of 49% compared with traditional priority queue structures, 
which validates the effectiveness of heterogeneous data structure fusion. After modifying three classic priority-flood 
variants (Wang & Liu, Barnes, and Zhou), the HRBTree demonstrates strong generalizability. Specifically, on billion-
scale datasets, the HRBTree-optimized Wang & Liu algorithm achieves a 45.6% speedup (average 35.1%), the Barnes 
algorithm improves by up to 37.6%, and the Zhou algorithm reaches a 28.2% speedup, confirming the structure’s 
compatibility with diverse algorithmic frameworks. This study provides critical insights for the engineering applica­
tion of terrain analysis algorithms and lays the foundation for next-generation high-performance, scalable computing 
paradigms in terrain analysis systems.

Introduction
DEMs represent fundamental datasets for digital terrain 
analysis, providing critical quantitative parameters (e.g., 
slope, curvature, and topographic wetness index) that serve as 
essential inputs for surface process simulations, including flood 
routing modelling, soil erosion assessment (e.g., RUSLE), and 
drainage network analysis (Jiang et al. 2023; Aristizabal et al. 
2023; Zhang et al. 2014; Fisher and Tate 2006; Wu et al. 2008; 
Zeng et al. 2020; Rajib et al. 2020; Mesa-Mingorance and 
Ariza-López 2020). The inherent presence of digital depres­
sions in DEMs significantly impacts the reliability of surface 
process simulation results (Wohl et al. 2018; Barnes et al. 2021). 
Unlike natural depressions with dynamic overflow mecha­
nisms, the discretized grid structure introduces topological 
discontinuities in flow paths, leading to systematic errors in 
flow accumulation calculations based on flow-direction algo­
rithms (Wang et al. 2019; Barták 2009; Barnes et al. 2020).
Depression processing constitutes a critical preprocess­
ing step in DEM-based modelling by ensuring that each grid 
cell maintains at least one hydrologically valid path to the 
DEM boundary. Numerous classical algorithms have been 
developed for this purpose (Peucker and Douglas 1975; 
Mark, 1984; O’callaghan and Mark 1984; Lindsay, 
2020; Lindsay and Creed 2005, 2006; Zhang et al. 2000; 
Śliwiński et al. 2022). With technological advancements, 
DEM resolution has improved from traditional 30-metre 
scales to contemporary sub-metre precision. High-res­
olution DEMs enable more detailed terrain representa­
tion but generate massive datasets (up to billions of 
grid cells), which present new computational challenges 
to algorithm performance and adaptability (Stocker-
waldhuber et al., 2017; Lindsay 2016; Su et al. 2015). 
The seminal Jenson and Domingue (1988) algorithm, 
with its O(N²) time complexity, has become inadequate 
for processing modern large-scale datasets (Jenson and 
Domingue 1988; Arnold 2010). To meet the requirements 
of working with big data, significant progress has been 
made in algorithmic optimization (Barnes et al. 2020; 
Zandbergen 2010; Lindsay 2020). Among these develop­
ments, the priority queue-based priority-flood algorithm 
has emerged as the most efficient foundational approach 
for depression filling (Wang and Liu 2006). Originally 
proposed by Ehlschlaeger (1989), this algorithm demon­
strates superior performance in both time complexity and 
memory efficiency (Barnes et al. 2014). The algorithm’s 
core workflow consists of three key operations: (1) insert­
ing all boundary cells into an elevation-sorted priority 
queue, (2) extracting and processing the lowest-elevation 
cell from the queue, and (3) examining the 8-connected 
neighbours of the processed cell and updating the queue 
accordingly.
The priority-flood algorithm was initially developed for 
watershed boundary delineation. Wang and Liu (2006) first 
adapted it for depression-filling applications (Wang & Liu 
algorithm) (Jiang et al. 2023). Due to its straightforward 
logic and ease of implementation, the Wang & Liu algo­
rithm has become the canonical version of the priority-flood 
algorithm (Metz et al. 2011). However, there remains room 
for optimization in terms of the data sorting efficiency of its 
priority queue and processing capacity (Wei et al. 2019). 
With the emergence of billion-cell DEM datasets, improv­
ing the computational efficiency of the priority-flood algo­
rithm has become a research priority.
Reducing the data volume in priority queues represents a 
crucial optimization direction for priority-flood algorithms. 
Barnes et al. (2014) achieved this by introducing a secondary 
regular queue to store depression cells, thereby decreasing 
the priority queue’s workload (Barnes et al. 2014; Barnes 
2016). Although this method improved computational effi­
ciency by only 15% compared to the Wang & Liu algorithm, 
it pioneered the concept of raster classification processing. 
Zhou et al. (2016) refined this mechanism, significantly 
reducing the number of cells processed by the priority queue 
(Zhou et al. 2017). Wei et al. (2019) conducted an in-depth 
analysis of the depression cell queuing mechanism, achiev­
ing a 70% reduction in priority queue data volume (Wei et 
al. 2019). Cordonnier et al. (2019) transformed the prior­
ity queue problem into a node-based graph search problem, 
completely eliminating the efficiency constraints imposed 
by priority queues (Cordonnier et al. 2019; Mankowitz et 
al. 2023). However, this approach demonstrates strong ter­
rain dependency, showing inferior performance to that of 
Barnes’ method in depression-dense areas.
Although existing methods have significantly reduced 
the data volume in priority queues, they remain inadequate 
for handling billion-cell DEM grids (Du et al. 2024). The 
microsecond-level single operations of priority queues still 
accumulate noticeable latency after billions of iterations, 
making optimization of their data structures crucial (Hendriks 
2010). Bai et al. (2015) recognized the inefficiency of priority 
queue sorting and adopted balanced binary trees (AVL trees) to 
improve queue sorting (Bai et al. 2015); however, the frequent 
balance maintenance led to increased memory overhead.
Notably, the current priority-flood algorithm has been 
implemented in parallel design, yet existing parallel 
solutions are mostly based on single path implementations 
of algorithm variations. Research efforts to increase 
the efficiency of monolithic algorithms remain highly 
important. Although the priority-flood algorithm and its 
variants have achieved fast computational efficiency, its 
priority queue still employs conventional sorting methods. 
Confronted with terabyte-scale DEM data, overcoming the 
dual bottleneck of priority queue size and sorting efficiency

Data and methods
The time complexity of the priority-flood algorithm is 
independent of the DEM resolution as well as the spatial 
distribution and connectivity characteristics of depres­
sions in the data; however, the algorithm’s computational 
efficiency is significantly constrained by the performance of 
the data structures employed.
HRBTree
Heap, which is a common priority queue, is commonly 
used in the priority-flood algorithm and typically achieves 
good performance; however, there is room for efficiency 
improvements. Some researchers have replaced the heap 
with an AVL tree to increase the algorithm’s efficiency 
(Bai et al. 2015).
A Red-Black Tree (RBTree), as a self-balancing binary 
search tree‌ (Bayer 1972; Guibas and Sedgewick  1978), 
maintains O(log N) query performance through a com­
bination of relaxed balancing conditions and colour tag­
ging with rotation rules while reducing the time cost of 
structural adjustments. However, fractal theory dem­
onstrates that natural terrain inherently possesses self-
similar characteristics, resulting in DEM data containing 
extensive repeated elevation values (Fig. 1). Barnes et al. 
(2014) reported that when data are inserted into a prior­
ity queue when its elevation value exactly matches that of 
the currently processed cell, the computation is essentially 
redundant; due to the heap property of the priority queue, 
the newly inserted element will be immediately popped, 
which does not change the queue state or affect subsequent 
computations (Barnes et al. 2014). This finding reveals 
the inefficiency of sorting such data. However, when an 
RBTree handles nodes with identical elevation values, the 
rotations (left-rotate/right-rotate) and colour adjustments 
required to maintain balance not only fail to improve the 
algorithm’s accuracy but also introduce an O(log n) level 
of additional time complexity. This demonstrates a nega­
tive relationship between the amount of consumed com­
puting resources and the benefits obtained.
‌HRBTree‌ is a hybrid data structure combining ‌hash tables‌ 
and RBTree‌. The hash tables store nodes that are grouped 
by priority, and the RBTree maintains ordered sequences 
across different priority levels. Utilizing a ‌memory pool‌ 
to pre-allocate node memory reduces the frequency of tree 
restructuring caused by repetitive terrain patterns while pre­
serving the query efficiency of priority queues (Fig. 2).
(1)	 The hash map is a fundamental data structure in computer 
science that supports efficient record access by map­
ping keys to specific locations via a hash function, 
achieving an average time complexity of O(1) for 
queries.
H(spill) = spill/1.00 
(1)
	
where spill represents the elevation value of the grid 
cell, which is a priority in the priority-flood algorithm.
(2)	 Bucket Storage: Floating-point priorities (e.g., eleva­
tion values) are mapped to different buckets via hash 
functions. Each bucket employs a linked list to store 
nodes sharing identical priority values (spill values), 
totalling m distinct priority levels. This clustered stor­
age of same-priority nodes reduces the RBTree node 
count (only needing to maintain keys for buckets with 
different priorities).
(3)	 Priority Order Maintenance with RBTree: Each RBTree 
node corresponds to a hash bucket’s spill-linked list, 
enabling rapid global minimum localization. This 
design ensures that the tree depth depends solely on 
unique priority count (m) rather than total node count 
(n), reducing the complexity from O(log n) to O(log 
m) and significantly decreasing the tree operation 
frequency.

For this experiment, we selected a typical depression-
dense area in Minnesota, USA (known as the “Land of 
10,000 Lakes”) as the study region. High-precision LiDAR 
DEM data (with resolutions ranging from 1 to 3 m; sourced 
from: http://www.mngeo.state.mn.us) for this region were 
integrated with partial MERIT DEM data (with a resolu­
tion of 90 m) (Yamazaki et al. 2017; Shin et al. 2020). This 
integration resulted in the construction of 19 test datasets 
spanning from million- to billion-cell grid scales (Table 2). 
The largest dataset contains up to 1.89 billion grid cells, 
effectively simulating ultra-large-scale terrain processing 
scenarios encountered in practical engineering applications.
The experimental platform is equipped with an Intel Core 
i7-14700 processor (2.10 GHz) and 64 GB DDR5 memory, 
and the algorithm is implemented in C++. Notably, the bench­
mark algorithm code is based on the open source project 
of Zhou et al. (2016) (​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​g​i​t​h​u​b​.​c​o​m​/​z​h​o​u​g​u​i​y​u​n​-​u​e​s​t​c​/​

priority-flood algorithm integrated with an HRBTree struc­
ture to reveal the critical disparities between theoretical 
complexity and engineering performance in terrain process­
ing algorithms.

This is primarily because the computational overhead of

highlights the need to find a balance between tree struc­

during algorithm design and selection. Theoretically, the 
data volume within the priority queue of the Barnes algo­
rithm is larger than that of the Zhou algorithm, which is 
validated by the results shown in Table 3. The Barnes 
algorithm reaches its balance point at approximately 1bil­
lion data points, whereas the Zhou algorithm achieves its 
balance point at approximately 200million. This thor­
oughly demonstrates that the structural adjustments of 
the RBTree have a measurable impact on computational 
efficiency.

units are processed, the efficiency of the priority queue 
decreases significantly. The underlying mechanism of the 
decline is the fragmentation generated by the contiguous 
array storage of the priority queue due to the expansion 
strategies that the traditional priority-flood algorithm uses 
to handle large-scale data, which leads to structural imbal­

adversely affect computational efficiency and cause exces­
sive memory consumption. In contrast, structures such as 
RBTree and HRBTree demonstrate unique advantages in 
this context.
RBTree structures theoretically possess advantages in

Conclusions
Our research focuses on the latter by introducing an HRB­
Tree‌ structure, which combines the rapid indexing of hash 
tables with the dynamic balancing properties of RBTree. 
This hybrid design significantly improves priority queue 
sorting efficiency. The experimental results confirm that 
priority-flood variants incorporating this structure exhibit 
substantial performance gains.
(1)	 Hybrid Indexing Mechanism Breakthrough‌.
	
The HRBTree structure demonstrates exceptional per­
formance in ultra-large datasets (> 1 billion nodes), 
achieving speedups of ‌45.6%‌ and ‌49%‌ over traditional 
RBTree and priority queues, respectively. These results 
validate the efficacy of heterogeneous data structure 
integration.

Abstract: Depression detection in digital terrain analysis is crucial for surface process modelling. High-resolution satellite imagery has led to an increasing demand for processing ultra-large-scale digital elevation models (DEMs) with billions of grid cells, which has exposed the computational inefficiencies of traditional priority-flood algorithms based on priority queues. While existing research has primarily focused on reducing the data volume in priority-flood’s priority queues, few studies have focused on optimizing the sorting mechanism within these queues. In this paper, we propose a hybrid Hash Red Black Tree (HRBTree) data structure, integrating the efficient insertion capability of hash tables with the ordered key-value maintenance of the RBTree, thereby reconstructing the priority queue architecture of the priority-flood algorithm. Using multi-scale DEM datasets ranging from millions to 1.6 billion grid cells, we systematically evaluated the computational efficiency of the enhanced priority-flood algorithm across varying data scales. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed HRBTree structure exhibits superior adaptability, particularly in ultra-large-scale datasets (> 1 billion nodes), achieving a maximum speedup of 49% compared with traditional priority queue structures, which validates the effectiveness of heterogeneous data structure fusion. After modifying three classic priority-flood variants (Wang & Liu, Barnes, and Zhou), the HRBTree demonstrates strong generalizability. Specifically, on billion- scale datasets, the HRBTree-optimized Wang & Liu algorithm achieves a 45.6% speedup (average 35.1%), the Barnes algorithm improves by up to 37.6%, and the Zhou algorithm reaches a 28.2% speedup, confirming the structure’s compatibility with diverse algorithmic frameworks. This study provides critical insights for the engineering applica­ tion of terrain analysis algorithms and lays the foundation for next-generation high-performance, scalable computing paradigms in terrain analysis systems.
